It was shaped like a lentil seed, thin in the middle and thick at the edge.
It was made by melting lentil seeds into the glass.
It had the colour of a lentil seed, so light passed through it easily.

questions.q:
Read three statements about the early microscopes.
Statement I: Robert Hooke's microscope made things look 200 to 300 times bigger than they look to the unaided eye.
Statement II: In the 1660s, the Dutch scientist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made better lenses, which let him build more useful microscopes.
Statement III: Robert Hooke's book Micrographia was a book of written notes only, with no drawings of what he saw.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only
o: I and II only
I only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: (a) Name the book that Robert Hooke published in 1665. (b) What did he call each of the small, empty spaces he saw in a thin slice of cork?
questions.a: (a) Micrographia. (b) He called each small space a cell.
s: (a) Names the book Micrographia
(b) States that he called each space a cell

questions.q: True or False? 'A curved piece of glass was called a lens because, like a lentil seed, it is thin in the middle and thick at the edge.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The piece of glass was shaped like a lentil seed, but it is thick in the middle and thin at the edge; that lentil shape is why it was called a lens.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a lens, like a lentil seed, is thick in the middle and thin at the edge

questions.q: Answer in one line each about Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. (a) Which country's scientist was he? (b) What did he make that let him build more useful microscopes? (c) Name two tiny things he was the first person to clearly see and describe.
questions.a: (a) He was a Dutch scientist (from the Netherlands). (b) Better lenses. (c) Bacteria and blood cells.
s: (a) States that he was a Dutch scientist
(b) States that he made better lenses
(c) Names bacteria and blood cells

questions.q: Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek both used microscopes in the 1660s. (a) What did Hooke see in the thin slice of cork, and what did Leeuwenhoek see? (b) State one contribution of each to science. (c) Using (a) and (b), explain why Leeuwenhoek, and not Hooke, is called the Father of Microbiology.
questions.a: (a) Hooke saw many small, empty spaces like a honeycomb in the cork; Leeuwenhoek saw tiny living things such as bacteria and blood cells. (b) Hooke published detailed drawings in Micrographia and first used the word cell in science; Leeuwenhoek made better lenses and more useful microscopes. (c) Leeuwenhoek was the first person to clearly see and describe tiny living things like bacteria, while Hooke's cork spaces were empty compartments, not tiny living organisms; that first description of microbes is why Leeuwenhoek gets the title.
s: (a) Hooke: empty, honeycomb-like spaces in cork; Leeuwenhoek: bacteria and blood cells
(b) Hooke: Micrographia drawings and the word cell; Leeuwenhoek: better lenses and microscopes
(c) Leeuwenhoek first clearly described tiny living things such as bacteria; Hooke's spaces were empty compartments

questions.q:
For a 'How we first saw cells' corner, a science centre in Kolkata wants visitors to sketch a thin slice of cork, as Robert Hooke did. Each cork compartment is about 0.04 mm across, and a visitor can sketch a compartment only if it looks at least 5 mm wide. The centre has Rs 5,000 and three choices: a water-filled round-bottom flask (free, makes things look about 2 times bigger), a hand magnifying glass (Rs 300, about 10 times bigger) and a replica of Hooke's microscope (Rs 4,500).
(a) From the chapter, how many times bigger did Hooke's microscope make things look?
(b) How wide does one compartment look through the magnifying glass? Can a visitor sketch it?
(c) What is the smallest width one compartment can look through the Hooke replica? Can a visitor sketch it?
(d) The manager says: 'Buy the magnifying glass. It is cheaper, and any lens makes things look bigger.' Decide which choice the centre should make, and justify it with your numbers.
questions.a: (a) 200 to 300 times. (b) 0.04 x 10 = 0.4 mm, which is less than 5 mm, so a visitor cannot sketch it. (c) 0.04 x 200 = 8 mm (up to 0.04 x 300 = 12 mm), which is more than 5 mm, so a visitor can sketch it. (d) Buy the Hooke replica. The flask (0.04 x 2 = 0.08 mm) and the magnifying glass (0.4 mm) both leave a compartment far below 5 mm, so the cheaper choices fail the task; even at its lowest, the replica gives 8 mm, and its Rs 4,500 is within the Rs 5,000. The manager is right that a lens makes things bigger, but a simple lens does not make them big enough; this is why lenses had to be improved into microscopes.
s: (a) 200 to 300 times
(b) 0.4 mm; less than 5 mm, so it cannot be sketched
(c) 8 mm at the least; more than 5 mm, so it can be sketched
(d) Chooses the replica: flask 0.08 mm and glass 0.4 mm are below 5 mm, replica at least 8 mm and Rs 4,500 is within Rs 5,000

questions.q:
Match each part of a cell in Column I with its job in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Cell membrane | a. Gives rigidity and strength to plants
2. Cytoplasm | b. Regulates all activities and the growth of the cell
3. Nucleus | c. The place where most life processes take place
4. Cell wall | d. A porous layer that lets in materials needed for life and lets out waste
Which matching is correct?

Assertion (A): Onion peel cells look firm and are arranged compactly with each other.
Reason (R): The cell membrane is porous and allows the entry of materials essential for life processes.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: (a) What is the cytoplasm of a cell? (b) Name any two compounds that the cytoplasm contains.
questions.a: (a) The cytoplasm is the material that fills the space between the cell membrane and the nucleus; most life processes take place in it. (b) Any two of carbohydrates, proteins, fats and mineral salts.
s: (a) Fills the space between the cell membrane and the nucleus (where most life processes happen)
(b) Names two of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, mineral salts

questions.q: True or False? 'Plastids are found only in the green parts of a plant, because their only job is photosynthesis.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Cells in all parts of a plant have plastids. Some plastids, like chloroplasts, contain chlorophyll and help in photosynthesis, while in non-green parts plastids help in the storage of substances.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: plastids are in all parts of a plant; chloroplasts help photosynthesis, plastids in non-green parts store substances

questions.q: Dev writes in his notebook: 'The cell membrane separates one cell from another, and it lets nothing pass through it.' Is Dev right, wrong or partly right? Explain, using what the chapter says the cell membrane does.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is right: the cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus and separates one cell from another. The second part is wrong: the membrane is porous, and it allows the entry of materials essential for life processes and the exit of waste material. A membrane that let nothing pass would starve the cell and trap its waste.
s: Verdict: partly right; the membrane does separate one cell from another
Correction: the membrane is porous, so materials do pass through it
It lets in materials needed for life processes and lets out waste

questions.q: Arya is preparing an onion peel slide for her school's science exhibition. State why she uses each of these: (a) a few drops of safranin, (b) a second petri dish containing water, (c) a drop of glycerin over the peel, (d) blotting paper at the end.
questions.a: (a) Safranin gives the cells a pinkish colour so that they can be seen clearly. (b) The water rinses the peel and removes the extra stain. (c) Glycerin prevents the cells from drying and improves clarity for better viewing. (d) Blotting paper gently wipes off the extra glycerin around the edges of the coverslip.
s: (a) Safranin colours the cells pink so they can be seen clearly
(b) Water rinses off the extra stain
(c) Glycerin stops the cells drying and improves clarity
(d) Blotting paper wipes off extra glycerin at the coverslip edges

questions.q: In a thought experiment, five cells from a green leaf, P, Q, R, S and T, are each missing a different one of these parts: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, chloroplasts, vacuole. P: materials needed for life processes cannot get in and waste cannot get out, yet the cell still keeps a rigid, firm outline. Q: the cell still takes in materials, but its activities are no longer regulated and it stops growing. R: the cell is not green and cannot help the leaf in photosynthesis. S: the cell has no large central space in which to store important substances. T: the cell still stores substances in its large central space, but it is no longer rigid and the cells around it do not stay packed closely together. Name the missing part in each cell and give the clue that rules out the other parts.
questions.a: P: cell membrane. The membrane is porous and controls the entry of needed materials and the exit of waste; the firm outline shows the cell wall is still present, so the wall is not the missing part. Q: nucleus. The nucleus regulates all activities in the cell and its growth; since materials still enter, the membrane is present. R: chloroplasts. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which makes them green and helps in photosynthesis; no other listed part makes the cell green. S: vacuole. The large, empty-looking vacuole stores important substances. T: cell wall. The cell wall gives rigidity and strength, which is why plant cells look firm and are packed compactly; the large central space is still there, so the vacuole is not the missing part.
s: P: cell membrane; entry and exit stopped while the rigid outline shows the wall is present
Q: nucleus; it regulates activities and growth, and entry of materials shows the membrane is present
R: chloroplasts; they hold chlorophyll, make the cell green and help in photosynthesis
S: vacuole; the large central space that stores substances is missing
T: cell wall; lost rigidity and compact packing while the vacuole is still present

questions.q: Imagine that a person's nerve cells were short and round, with no branches. What would most likely suffer, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Passing messages quickly around the body, which needs a long, branched shape

Nothing, since the shape of a cell has no link with the job it does

questions.q:
Match each kind of cell in Column I with the feature that suits its job in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Inner cheek cell | a. Long and branched, carries messages
2. Nerve cell | b. Thin, flexible and spindle-shaped, contracts and relaxes in waves
3. Food-pipe muscle cell | c. Thin and flat, forms a protective lining
4. Cell of the inner lining of the stomach | d. Produces digestive juices and acid
Which matching is correct?

Reason (R): Plant cells may be rectangular, elongated, oval or even tube-like.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: (a) What is a tissue? (b) What do different tissues form when they are organised together?
questions.a: (a) A tissue is a group of similar cells. (b) Different tissues organised together form an organ.
s: (a) A tissue is a group of similar cells
(b) Tissues organised together form an organ

questions.q: True or False? 'Several organs working together to perform a major function of the body form an organ system.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Several organs work together to form an organ system that performs a major function of the body; it is the level between organ and organism (for example, the digestive system, in which the food pipe and stomach work together in digestion).
s: Verdict: True
Reason: organs work together as an organ system for a major function, the level between organ and organism, with an example such as the digestive system

questions.q: Write the level of organisation (cell, tissue, organ, organ system or organism) for each of these: (i) a single nerve cell, (ii) a group of similar muscle cells in the wall of the food pipe, (iii) the stomach, (iv) the digestive system, (v) a goat, (vi) the yolk of an ostrich egg.
questions.a: (i) Cell. (ii) Tissue, since it is a group of similar cells. (iii) Organ, since it is made of different tissues (muscle cells that churn food and lining cells that make digestive juices). (iv) Organ system. (v) Organism. (vi) Cell, since the yolk of an ostrich egg is a single cell, the largest known cell.
s: (i) cell and (ii) tissue
(iii) organ and (iv) organ system
(v) organism and (vi) cell

questions.q:
In Ooty, Class 8 students stand the stalk of a white carnation in a glass of water coloured with red ink. After 6 hours, thin red lines run up the stalk and the edges of the petals turn pink. Under a microscope, a thin slice of the stalk shows rows of long, tube-like cells coloured red, surrounded by many oval and round cells that stay pale.
(a) Which job of plant cells does the red colour moving up the stalk show?
(b) Which cells did this job, judging by their shape?
(c) The pale cells have different shapes from the red ones. Which general idea from the chapter about cells does this support?
(d) Kiran concludes: 'Every cell in a plant carries water.' Do the students' observations support Kiran? Decide, and give your reasoning.
questions.a: (a) Some plant cells carry water throughout the plant. (b) The long, tube-like cells, since some plant cells form long tubes that carry water. (c) Plant cells vary in shape (rectangular, elongated, oval, tube-like), and the shape and structure of a cell suit the job it does. (d) No. Only the tube-like cells turned red; the oval and round cells around them stayed pale, so they did not carry the coloured water. The data show that water is carried by the tube-shaped cells, while cells of other shapes do other jobs.
s: (a) Some plant cells carry water through the plant
(b) The long, tube-like cells
(c) Plant cells vary in shape, and shape suits function
(d) Rejects Kiran's claim: only tube-like cells were red, the oval and round cells stayed pale

questions.q: Kiran makes clay models for a display called 'A cell's shape suits its job'. (a) Inner cheek cells: tall, thick and round. (b) A nerve cell: very long, with many branches. (c) Food-pipe muscle cells: thick, stiff and cube-shaped. (d) Plant cells that carry water: small, round and separate from each other. (e) The stomach: built only of muscle cells. For each model, say whether it matches the chapter. If it does not, say what it should show, and link your answer to the job these cells do.
questions.a: (a) Does not match. Inner cheek cells are thin and flat, which lets them form a protective lining on the inner surface of the cheek. (b) Matches. Nerve cells are long and branched, which helps them reach different parts of the body and pass on messages quickly. (c) Does not match. Food-pipe muscle cells are thin, flexible and spindle-shaped, so they can contract and relax in a wave-like manner and push food down to the stomach; stiff cubes could not do this. (d) Does not match. Some plant cells form long tubes that help carry water throughout the plant. (e) Does not match. The stomach has muscle cells in its wall that churn the food and other cells in its inner lining that produce digestive juices and acid; it needs both kinds.
s: (a) Wrong: cheek cells are thin and flat, forming a protective lining
(b) Right: long and branched to reach body parts and pass messages quickly
(c) Wrong: thin, flexible, spindle-shaped, to contract and relax in waves and push food
(d) Wrong: they form long tubes that carry water through the plant
(e) Wrong: wall muscle cells churn food; lining cells make digestive juices and acid

questions.q: (a) What are microorganisms? (b) Give one example of a unicellular microorganism and one example of a multicellular microorganism.
questions.a: (a) Microorganisms are living organisms made of just one or very few cells, so small that they cannot be seen with the naked eye. (b) Unicellular: bacteria or Amoeba. Multicellular: some fungi or some algae.
s: (a) Living things too small to see with the naked eye, made of one or very few cells
(b) One unicellular example (bacteria, Amoeba) and one multicellular example (some fungi or algae)

questions.q: True or False? 'Microorganisms can live only at moderate temperatures, like the ones people live in.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Microorganisms are found at moderate temperatures, but some can even be found in extreme climatic conditions, such as hot water springs and snow-cold zones.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: some microorganisms live in extreme conditions such as hot water springs and snow-cold zones

questions.q:
Meera sorts microorganisms into two boxes labelled 'one cell' and 'many cells'.
(a) Into which box should she put Amoeba, Paramecium and bacteria?
(b) In the class record of pond water, the alga seen was a single cell, but the chapter says some algae have many cells. Can the label 'algae' go into just one box? Explain.
(c) Name one other group of microorganisms from the chapter that also cannot go into just one box, and give a reason.
questions.a: (a) All three go into the 'one cell' box: Amoeba and Paramecium are single-celled protozoa and bacteria are unicellular. (b) No. The pond-water alga was a single cell, while some algae have many cells, so algae as a group belong in both boxes; each alga has to be placed by itself. (c) Fungi: some fungi have many cells (mould is a multicellular fungus) while yeast is a unicellular fungus.
s: (a) Amoeba, Paramecium and bacteria all in the 'one cell' box
(b) No: the pond alga was single-celled but some algae are many-celled, so algae fit both boxes
(c) Fungi, with the reason that yeast is unicellular while mould is multicellular

questions.q: A student's field notebook describes four organisms seen under a microscope. W (pond water): a single cell that moves from one place to another with the help of specialised structures and is not green. X (soil suspension): a branched filament without chlorophyll, with a sac-like structure. Y (soil suspension): a branched filament without chlorophyll, with a brush-like structure. Z (soil suspension): a spherical cell with chlorophyll, a green pigment. Name each organism and its group, and give the feature that decided it.
questions.a: W: Paramecium (Protozoa), a single moving cell that moves with specialised structures. X: Bread mould (Fungi), a branched filament without chlorophyll with a sac-like structure. Y: Mould (Fungi), a branched filament without chlorophyll with a brush-like structure. Z: Alga (Algae), spherical with chlorophyll; some bacteria are spherical too, but bacteria have no green pigment and have hair-like structures instead.
s: W: Paramecium (Protozoa), moves with specialised structures
X: Bread mould (Fungi), sac-like structure on a branched filament
Y: Mould (Fungi), brush-like structure on a branched filament
Z: Alga (Algae), spherical with chlorophyll; the green pigment rules out a spherical bacterium

questions.q: (a) What is decomposition? (b) Name one kind of waste, other than fruit and vegetable peels, that microorganisms decompose.
questions.a: (a) Decomposition is the process in which microorganisms break down complex substances, such as those in fallen leaves, into simpler substances that are rich in nutrients. (b) Any one: fallen leaves, bodies of dead animals, or animal waste such as dung.
s: (a) Microorganisms break complex substances into simpler, nutrient-rich ones
(b) Names fallen leaves, dead animal bodies or dung

questions.q: True or False? 'Yeast, which is used to make bread dough soft and fluffy, is a fungus.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Yeast is a type of microorganism that belongs to the group called fungi; as it breaks down food it releases carbon dioxide, whose bubbles make the dough soft and fluffy.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: yeast belongs to the fungi and releases carbon dioxide that makes the dough fluffy

questions.q: The chapter's 'Our scientific heritage' box is about tiny living things in ancient Indian texts. (a) What does the word 'Krimi' mean? (b) What do the words 'Drishya' and 'Adrishya' mean? (c) Name the Veda that the chapter says also refers to 'Krimi'.

s: (a) Krimi: different tiny entities
(b) Drishya: visible; Adrishya: invisible
(c) The Atharvaveda

questions.q:
A school in Dehradun tests three compost bins for 3 weeks. Each bin is half-filled with garden soil, gets 2 kg of fruit and vegetable peels, and is topped with a layer of soil. Bin X is watered to keep it moist and kept in the shade at about 28 °C; after 3 weeks the peels have turned into a dark-coloured material. Bin Y is never watered and kept beside Bin X at about 28 °C; its peels have dried up and are mostly unchanged. Bin Z is watered to keep it moist but kept in a cold store at about 8 °C; its peels are mostly unchanged.
(a) Name the two kinds of microorganisms in the soil that broke down the peels in Bin X.
(b) What is the dark-coloured material, and how does it help the soil?
(c) Compare Bins X and Y. What does this pair show?
(d) The gardener says: 'Moisture is all these microbes need; temperature does not matter.' Using all three bins, decide whether the data support him.
questions.a: (a) Fungi and bacteria. (b) It is manure, which is rich in nutrients and helps increase the fertility of the soil. (c) X and Y differ only in water, and only the moist bin made manure, so the microbes need moisture to decompose the peels. (d) No. Bin Z was as moist as Bin X but was cold, and its peels were mostly unchanged, so moisture alone is not enough; manure forms only at an optimal temperature together with the right amount of moisture.
s: (a) Fungi and bacteria
(b) Manure: rich in nutrients, increases soil fertility
(c) X and Y differ only in water, so moisture is needed
(d) Rejects the claim using Bin Z: moist but cold, no manure; needs optimal temperature and moisture

questions.q:
The chapter asks you to think what would happen if microorganisms did not exist on Earth. Analyse what would happen in each case, giving the reason from the chapter.
(a) Fallen leaves and the bodies of dead animals.
(b) The nutrients in the soil.
(c) Pea and bean crops grown without chemical fertilisers.
(d) Bread dough that bakers normally make rise by adding yeast.
(e) Lukewarm milk mixed with a spoonful of curd and kept in a warm place, as a family waits for curd.
questions.a: (a) They would not be decomposed and would pile up, since decomposition is done by microorganisms. (b) Nutrients would not go back to the soil, so plants would not grow as well. (c) There would be no Rhizobium in their root nodules to trap nitrogen from the air, so they would need chemical fertilisers and would no longer naturally increase the nitrogen in the soil. (d) The dough would not rise or become soft and fluffy, since yeast is itself a microorganism (a fungus); with no yeast, no carbon dioxide would be released to form bubbles. (e) The milk would not turn into curd, since the spoonful of curd would hold no Lactobacillus to feed on lactose and produce lactic acid.
s: (a) Waste would not be decomposed and would pile up
(b) Nutrients would not return to the soil; plants grow less well
(c) No Rhizobium to trap nitrogen in root nodules; soil nitrogen not raised naturally
(d) Yeast is a microorganism, so none is there to release carbon dioxide; dough does not rise
(e) No Lactobacillus to ferment lactose into lactic acid; no curd

questions.q: Meena's family in Chennai grinds idli batter at night, and by morning it has fermented and is ready. Her cousin in a cold hill town follows the same recipe in winter and finds the batter has hardly fermented by morning. (a) Name the bacterium that the chapter says helps ferment idli and dosa batter. (b) Using what the chapter says about how this bacterium grows, explain the cousin's result.
questions.a: (a) Lactobacillus. (b) Lactobacillus grows well in warm conditions. In the cold hill town in winter it multiplies and ferments slowly, so the batter has hardly fermented by morning, just as milk with curd kept in a cool place does not set into curd.
s: (a) Lactobacillus
(b) It grows well in warm conditions, so in the cold it ferments the batter slowly

questions.q:
A hostel warden in Madurai wants each of her 30 children to get 30 g of protein a day from one extra food, and she can spend at most Rs 600 a day on it. She compares two foods. A packet of moong dal says it has 24 g of protein in every 100 g and costs Rs 120 per kg. Dried Spirulina powder costs Rs 1,600 per kg.
(a) What kind of organism is Spirulina, and how does it get its food?
(b) Using the chapter, show that one child's 30 g of protein needs less than 50 g of Spirulina.
(c) How many grams of the dal give 30 g of protein?
(d) Which food should the warden choose to meet the whole protein target within Rs 600 a day? Justify with numbers, and say what she gives up by not choosing the other.
questions.a: (a) A microalga, a microscopic plant-like organism that makes its own food using sunlight. (b) Protein is more than 60 per cent of Spirulina's weight, so 50 g holds more than 0.6 x 50 = 30 g of protein; therefore less than 50 g is enough for 30 g. (c) 30 / 24 x 100 = 125 g. (d) Moong dal. The children need 30 x 30 = 900 g of protein a day. From dal this needs 900 / 24 x 100 = 3,750 g = 3.75 kg, costing 3.75 x 120 = Rs 450, within Rs 600. Rs 600 buys only 600 / 1,600 x 1,000 = 375 g of Spirulina, which gives more than 225 g of protein; reaching 900 g from 375 g would need Spirulina to be 240 per cent protein, which is impossible. By not choosing Spirulina she gives up its vitamin B12 and the small serving size (less than 50 g gives one child's 30 g of protein).
s: (a) A microalga that makes its own food using sunlight
(b) 50 g holds more than 30 g of protein (over 60 per cent), so less than 50 g is needed
(c) 125 g of dal
(d) Chooses dal: 900 g protein needs 3.75 kg dal = Rs 450; Rs 600 buys only 375 g Spirulina, far short of 900 g protein; notes the vitamin B12 given up

questions.q: Arjun argues that 'The cell is the basic unit of life' cannot be true, for three reasons. (i) An Amoeba has no tissues or organs, so one cell alone cannot be a complete living thing. (ii) In a human, a nerve cell cannot digest food and a muscle cell cannot carry messages, so no single cell is a unit of life. (iii) Yeast is one cell but mould has many cells, so fungi do not follow any one rule. Evaluate each of his reasons using the chapter, and then decide whether the statement still holds.
questions.a: (i) Not valid. Unicellular organisms such as Amoeba (and bacteria) carry out all the functions necessary for their survival in a single cell, so one cell can be a complete living thing. (ii) Not valid. In multicellular organisms, cells carry out specialised functions individually but cooperate with each other to increase the chance of survival; the body is still built of cells. (iii) Not valid. The rule is that all living beings are made of one or more cells; yeast (a unicellular fungus) and mould (a multicellular fungus) both fit it. Each cell contains components, such as the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus, that help the organism perform its functions and survive. So the statement holds: the bodies of all living organisms are made of cells, and Arjun's reasons show only that cells differ in number, shape and job.
s: (i) Rejects it: a unicellular organism carries out all functions for survival in one cell
(ii) Rejects it: in multicellular organisms cells specialise but cooperate; the body is still built of cells
(iii) Rejects it: all living beings are made of one or more cells; yeast and mould both fit
A cell contains components (membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus) that let it perform functions
Decides the statement holds: all bodies are made of cells; the reasons show only that cells differ
